paras: The lynching of Kit Jackson and Harry Russell was the shooting of three Black men by four white men near Hope Hull, at McGehee's Switch in Montgomery County, Alabama, early on August 18, 1915; Jackson and Harry Russell were killed and Ed Russell was left for dead. The three were free on bond on an untried charge of poisoning livestock. Wire reports carried it nationally as the lynching of three men, and Black weeklies cited it as a case that drew little notice beside the lynching of Leo Frank the day before.

According to the Montgomery Advertiser, the three had been arrested in June on a charge of poisoning horses on Dr. McLean's plantation, where they then lived; a fourth man, Alex Jackson, was still jailed, and the case had never come to trial. A Montgomery dispatch said the animals were mules, alleged that the men had begun "a crusade of arson and poison" after being replaced by white tenants, and said their release on bond the day before the killing "infuriated the white farmers."

Testimony at the coroner's inquest described four white men who drove to the Crenshaw plantation, forced a resident to guide them, and enforced darkness and silence with revolvers. They tied the hands of Kit Jackson and the two Russells, took them from their homes and drove off toward Montgomery. Between three and four o'clock pistol shots woke Ed Crenshaw, and a search party found the men in a roadside ditch, Harry Russell and Kit Jackson dead. Ed Russell, hit five times, was taken to Montgomery by Sheriff Waller.

Governor Henderson ordered an investigation the same day and said he might call a special grand jury. The coroner's inquest heard five witnesses and adjourned until Ed Russell, under guard in a hospital with a broken hip, could testify. The Advertiser reported that Black residents were afraid to speak for fear of a mob and that an exodus from the neighborhood was predicted. On August 20 the governor offered $350 each for the conviction of those responsible for "the murder of Kit Jackson and Harry Russell, or for assault with intent to murder Ed Russell." No report of arrests, a grand jury or a trial appears in the coverage.

White papers ran the story on August 18 as a short wire item, under headlines such as "Two Negroes Lynched" in the Washington Evening Star and "Three Negroes Lynched" in the Keokuk Daily Gate City. One brief added that "the evidence is said to have been strong against them," and the Richmond Virginian headed its copy "Alabama and Georgia Vie in Lynchings."

The Montgomery Advertiser wrote of "mobmen" in its news columns, but its editorial page said "Four men can hardly be called a mob" and called the killing "an outbreak of neighborhood feud." Elsewhere, the Washington Evening Star wrote that "The law was lynched along with the three negroes," and editorials in the Monroe Journal and the Guthrie Daily Leader set the killing over mules beside Frank's death to mock Southern "chivalry."

Black weeklies reprinted the three-line dispatch and made the gap in attention their theme. The New York Age, in an editorial the Omaha Monitor reprinted, wrote that the item appeared "in an equally modest place in several papers" while the Frank case filled the dailies. The Philadelphia Tribune stressed that the men were "accused (but had no trial)," the Oakland Sunshine headed its note "Mules More Valuable Than Negroes," and the Plaindealer predicted that no one would "even condemn the diabolical deed."

The Advertiser, which followed the inquest, reported two dead and Ed Russell alive, and the governor's reward named an assault on him rather than a murder. Wire versions said the third man died in a hospital or that all three were lynched, and named the dead "Kid" Jackson with Henry or Frank Russell. One Alaska brief said the men were taken from jail and hanged, which the local accounts of a seizure at home and a shooting contradict.

reader.title: Lynching of Kit Jackson and Harry Russell
bases: Four white men took three Black men accused of poisoning livestock from their homes at night, bound them and shot them, killing two (A5, A1, A14).

Four white men with no lawful authority seized and shot three Black men free on bond on a charge of poisoning livestock, killing at least two (A5, A7, A14); papers called it a lynching and linked it to the charge (A1, A4, A12).
The local Montgomery Advertiser (A5, A11, A14), a Birmingham special (A7) and independent wire services (A1, A4) agree on the seizure and shooting, though they differ on whether two or three died.

framing.detail: Out-of-state dailies ran short Montgomery dispatches headed 'Two Negroes Lynched' or 'Three Negroes Lynched'.
The Montgomery Advertiser reported the 'mobmen' and the investigation closely but editorially called it a 'neighborhood feud' and defended Alabama against comparison with Georgia.
The Washington Evening Star's 'Government by Law, or "Clan"?' said 'The law was lynched'; the Monroe Journal and Guthrie Daily Leader satirized Southern chivalry.
The New York Age, Philadelphia Tribune, Plaindealer and Oakland Sunshine used the case to show white indifference to Black victims beside the Frank lynching.
The Afro-American, Philadelphia Tribune and Richmond Planet ran the wire briefs.
